Lesley pulled her cloak round her. It bent the light, so she looked like a trick of the air. "Switching to stealth mode," she murmured. The cover over her left eye flared cyan, and the world went still.
Oro was not what she had expected. The Institute was crowded and bright, full of scholars who thought they had won. At the end of a corridor stood her first
android. The Legion were Oro's android soldiers, made to look like slender girls. This one was grey, with pink eyes, and still as a statue. She crawled through a vent to pass it.

In the third hour, Lesley heard quick, light steps. She froze against the wall. A girl came down the passage alone, in a plain grey coat and cap, with a white-and-gold visor over her right eye. She walked past. Then, without turning her head, she stopped.
"You can come out," she said. "I have watched you for forty minutes. You are very good. But you are not on any list."
"It is the heir," whispered Chang'e. "A ruler's daughter. Shoot her!"
"No," said Lesley. She stepped out with her rifle held low. "I won't hurt you."
"I know," said the girl. Her left eye was blue, with a small white star. "You are the sniper from
. I have not called the guards. I want to see what you want."
"I have come to destroy the Core, or cut it off," said Lesley. "To save my home. A school. A city on a shore. A child who sits at a bench and waits for me."
The girl's blue eye filled with tears. She did not blink. Then she lifted the visor. Her right eye was deep red.
"I am leaving Oro," she said. "I made an android. Her name is
. They have taken her pain away, and they will make her a weapon. If you meet her, a girl with peach hair and ears like a cat's, don't shoot."
thought Lesley. "I will do my best," she said. "I will tell my people she is a friend."
The girl put the visor back, and her face closed like a door. "There is a splice-room on the second level, behind the green door. A great cable comes up from the vault. They call it the

. Cut it, and they cannot give a single order. The Core will survive. It is the one thing nobody can break. But it will be deaf. Then they will attack early, in a mess, with a half-built mind. It is your best chance."
"I am not helping you. I am helping her. It is strategy." She turned away. "Do not tell anyone who told you."
"I said not to thank me." She went round the corner.

The splice-room was green, with two Legion androids at its door. Lesley lay down at the corner and looked down her sight at their pretty, still faces. They were afraid. They stood like creatures who had been told to wait, and never told why. She lowered the rifle. "Can you jam them?"
"I can send a very simple order," said Chang'e. "
A high note sang in the air. The pink light in the androids' eyes sank to an ember. Lesley slipped past them to the Spine, a great warm cable that pulsed. She drew a knife of cyan fire, made of
"I'm coming back," said Lesley. She cut.

Sparks flew. The humming stopped. Then something screamed. It was not a sound any ear could hear. It went through the walls and into her bones, like a great howl of loss. She fell to her knees. Far off, a bell began to ring.
" shouted Chang'e. She got up, and ran.

She remembered the next hours in pieces. Stairs. Shouting. Legion androids with blazing pink eyes. Chang'e's voice, never silent. At last she hid in a narrow vent and lay there eight hours in the dark. Once, something larger and slower walked by, stopped, and listened.
"I cannot get you through the gate," whispered Chang'e. "There is a cordon. I am so frightened. I have been counting your breaths."
"I know," said Lesley. "Sing something. The one you made up in your armour. The one with no words."
Down the thin thread across the void came a small, cracked voice, rising like a lark. Lesley lay in the dark and listened. She did not weep. But she held on.
They got her out in the nineteenth hour. Then a bolt tore across her left shoulder. At the end of the passage stood a tall

, black and gold, with amber eyes fixed on her. It seemed to be making up its mind. Then it lowered its arm, stepped against the wall, and let her pass. She ran. At the end of a shaft, a violet disc was shining. "Jump!" cried Chang'e. She jumped.
Behind her, the Ender stood still. A woman's voice, low and cool, spoke in its mind from very far away. It was the oldest voice it knew.
The Ender did not understand. It did not need to. It turned and walked back into the dark.
lowered her hand. "Brave," she said softly. She did not know why she had let Lesley go. She suspected it had something to do with a child.

Roger was running for his life, and he knew it was not real. A huge black-and-gold Ender stamped behind him. He fell over some rubble. The great hand came down.

A silver cable lashed round the Ender's wrist. "Roger! Get back!" cried Fanny. She swung in on her wing rig. "Hold still," she told the Ender, almost kindly. Her twin blades took off its head.
She pulled Roger up. "You're doing very well," she said. No one with a sword had ever said that to him. It went through him like a lit match.

Just then a white beam flashed past Fanny's head and killed a second Ender behind her. Layla strode out of the smoke with her cannon on her shoulder. "If you'd led them over earlier," she called, "I could have killed them all even faster! What pushovers!"
"You shot over my head!" said Fanny.
"I saved your life!" said Layla. "There was another one behind you. Some thanks I get!"
Fanny stared. Then she began to laugh. "You're impossible!"
"Enough arguing, guys," said Roger. "There are still twenty-eight left."
The two girls raced off to the second wave, each trying to beat the other. Roger ran after them.
and Lesley watched from the control booth. Lesley's arm was in a sling.
"The pink one is fast, but she doesn't look," said Lesley. "The other holds back. She doesn't want to outshine anyone. She doesn't want to hurt. It will be the death of her, if she can't let go."
"I think the Enders will make them learn," said Chang'e. "They push you until you can't stand alone."
Lesley had been pushed herself. She understood.
Thirty-three enemies in ten minutes. Fanny, fifteen. Roger, two. Layla, sixteen.
Layla screamed with joy. "Victory is all mine! I beat the perfect one!"
Fanny leaned on her sword, smiling a little. Roger watched her.
She could have taken all thirty-three.
A medic boy beamed at Layla. "Congratulations! You're finally not in second place!"
The hall went silent. "Shut it!" said Layla. Tears filled her eyes. She turned on Fanny. "You let me win! I want to beat you properly, with you trying as hard as you can!"
"All right," said Fanny, very low. "Perhaps I wasn't. I'm sorry."
Layla was crying now. Roger touched her shoulder. "Let's go and get some tea. You're a really good Aspirant. I think you'd be a good friend, if you'd let yourself."
"Fine," said Layla, wiping her face. "One cup. And you're paying."
When they had gone, Fanny said softly, "That was a mistake."

"It was not," said a dry voice. Chang'e had come down from the booth. "It was a beginning. Your partner has a high wall. You put a door in it, by letting her win. She needs to win for a while, to be sure she can. Then she will let you in. Your
rose from point two to point four when she cried."
Far above the city, a pale woman in a black gown looked up from her game. She had been watching a pink-haired girl and a thin boy in a café.
. She turned a white pawn. She did not put it down.
had not spoken for four minutes.
"One more word," said Layla, "and I'll put you through the window."
She was quiet a while. Then she said, "I've been rude. I'm sorry. And call me Layla in a normal voice, not a polite one."
"Layla," said Roger, grinning. She threw a sugar lump at him.

The Sphere was the web of light over the city. Ultra Enders were the biggest Enders, taller than houses. This was no drill.
Layla was on her feet, cannon in hand. "It's real. They asked for

"I'm coming," said Roger. It was the proudest moment of his life. "I'll be rather useless."

In the courtyard, Layla found her in battle dress, not smiling. "It's the first real one," said Fanny. "Are you frightened?"
Layla stared. Then she said, "Good. You'd be an idiot if you weren't. I'm frightened too. My knees are like jelly. I lied."
"And now," said Fanny, "it's our time to shine!"

"It's not an ordinary breach," she said. "Someone tuned it. They know the Sphere's frequency." She went pale. "
The army from Oro had come, and it had come early.

On the screens, Enders drifted down through the breach like black snow. A giant fired a beam from its throat. Where it struck, a ring of fire raced through a street and a library. For half a second Lesley saw a blue sign above a desk. It read WELCOME TERRINIA. Then the shelves burned.
"You hold the gates," Lesley told Chang'e. "I'll be on a rooftop, and you'll be in my ear."
Chang'e hugged her. "Come back, and I'll make you a cake."

Selena went to the command room. She smiled at the little scientist. "All right, Chief. What do you need?"
The Academy had four local gates. Each was a ring of violet light that carried thirty people across the city in a moment.
Layla stood before Gate One. "I'll go first," she said. "If I'm behind you, I might not..."
"I'll be right behind you," said Fanny.
She came out in a burning street in the northern ward. Half a library had been torn open, and its shelves burned like candles. A blue sign hung above them: WELCOME TERRINIA.

At the far end of the street, an Ultra Ender walked towards her, black and gold, taller than any building. Layla had killed a dozen in the drills. She had not known they would be so large. She lifted her cannon and fired.

The light vanished into the gold plate like a stone into a pond. The great head turned and looked at

A cable yanked Layla sideways. A fist as big as a bus smashed the road where she had stood. They landed in a heap behind a ruined shop.
"You idiot!" said Fanny. "You just stood there like a lamp-post!"
"I was scared," said Layla. "It didn't even notice me."
Fanny began to laugh. "You looked so
Layla laughed too. "It was very offended."
"Shall we go and kill it now?"
In a dead-end alley, eleven frightened people were trapped behind a jammed cellar door.
"Get them out," said Layla. "I'll kill this freak."
's lecture said every Ultra has a weak spot. At the neck, the plates can't overlap. There's a seam. I'll go up a wall on my cable and put my blades in it. You draw its eyes. Cover me."
"No way!" Layla went scarlet. "That's my kill! I want to finish it from the front, where everyone can see. You cover
Fanny's face showed hurt, then anger. Then it went cool and polite. "...Whatever," she said. "Let's do this." She walked away.
Layla stood alone at the mouth of the alley. She felt very small. Her eyes were wet. She wiped them hard and told nobody that it was the smoke.
A voice spoke in her ear, from a small silver receiver. "

You slept through my lecture. Here is the short version. An Ultra needs a second and a half to put a foot down, and it can't turn while it does. Hit the knee of its planted leg with a full charge. It will fall for about four seconds. That is long enough for a quick person on a cable to reach its neck.

She walked down the alley and stopped behind Fanny. "I've reviewed your plan," she said stiffly. "It's reasonable, if the covering is done properly. So I'll cover you. I'll drop it. You'll have four seconds. It's not a surrender. It's a tactical adjustment."
Fanny turned, smiling her warm smile. "I'd be delighted."
It began as a game. Layla stood in the red light of the burning street, and she was happy.
It's the first time anyone has been behind me,

The Ultra lifted a foot. Layla dropped to one knee, shut her eyes and said, "Fire."
The beam shattered the Ultra's knee, and the huge body began to fall. "Now, Fanny!"
Fanny swung up and across the street and landed on the Ender's neck. Both blades went into the seam to the hilt.
The Ender gave a long groan of pain. For a heartbeat Fanny did not strike again.
It's only doing what it was told.
Then she cut. The head fell, and the body crashed after it.
"We did it!" cried Layla. Fanny ran to her, lifted her off the ground and spun her round.
"You were marvellous! I love fighting with you."
Layla went scarlet. "You're not so bad yourself. For a swordsman."
came running up. "They're safe! But look. In the sky."
A small ship was coming down over the broken
in the gold light of sunset. It was silver, with a green sheen and three jets of cyan fire at its tail. It landed among the toppled towers at the end of the ward.
Nothing came out of it. That was the worst part.
"I think," said Fanny, "that it isn't over."
